prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: Four of eight members ranked B015 first in the opening round, and the support rests on the science rather than on the count. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the lattice light shift while keeping the statistics of many atoms in parallel, and the strontium lattice clocks, brought to record accuracy and stability by Ye's group, are an invention with an unambiguous figure of merit. Independent groups on several continents, using Sr, Yb and Hg, have reproduced 10^-18-class performance, so the result is confirmed and not merely claimed. The downstream impact is concrete: tests of relativity and of varying constants, dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy and the ongoing process towards a redefinition of the second. The credit supports a clean two-laureate prize of a proposer-demonstrator and a precision-record holder, and no further name has to be forced in.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap. The 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for control of single trapped ions already honoured the enabling technology and the first-generation optical clocks, so the lattice clock can be read as an incremental, if brilliant, step on recognised ground. Competing lattice-clock groups at SYRTE, PTB, NIST and elsewhere, and the record-uncertainty sequence among them, are not carried by the two supplied names. The redefinition of the second is also still pending, and one can argue that the committee should wait for it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B015 only seventh and asked whether the field is already recognised through the frequency comb and ion-clock prizes, while putting twisted bilayer graphene (B017) first.
responses.response: I take the overlap question seriously, but I think it is answered by the physics. The comb provided the ruler and the ion-clock work provided single-quantum-system control. The lattice clock is a different measurement principle: a magic wavelength that cancels the trap shift, so that many atoms are interrogated at once and statistical power is gained at essentially no systematic cost. That is why stability moved by orders of magnitude, and it is a discovery-grade idea in its own right. I do agree that B017 is a strong, secure and timely discovery with a clean theory-plus-experiment split, and I rank it as my first alternative. My own reservation is only that the superconducting mechanism is still debated and that several early experimental contributors, including Yuan Cao, sit outside the three supplied names, which makes the credit less tidy than for B015.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B015 first as a clean two-name prize and ranked B016 second, proposing the experimental leaders Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger, with Zoller and Cirac as a theory-weighted alternative.
responses.response: I agree with her on B015, and her point that the other lattice-clock groups are not covered by the supplied credit is the one qualification I would also record. On B016 I part company in one respect. The five-name credit list forces an arbitrary cut, and a trio of experimentalists would leave the theoretical origin by Zoller, Cirac and Jaksch unrecognised, which I find harder to defend than the two-person cut for B015. A three-person B016 is a legitimate prize, and I keep it as a second alternative, but I would not prefer it while the allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac is so contested.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B012) first, disclosed that she works in this area, and noted that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits makes an immediate second prize in the same family a question.
responses.response: I respect the disclosure and I agree that circuit QED is very mature and widely replicated. But the proximity to the 2025 prize is a real argument for waiting, and so is the exclusion of Girvin from a three-person split of four credited names. Transmon-based architectures are also still reaching their payoff in quantum computing, so I do not think the case is stronger than B015 on either distinctness or credit. I would be willing to revisit it if the committee agrees that it is a separate discovery from the 2025 prize and has a defensible three-person split.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked the topological insulators and quantum spin Hall effect (B051) first, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and called recognition overdue.
responses.response: I accept that B051 is a conceptual change in how band structure is understood, and the near-two-decade record of confirmation is persuasive. My difficulty is attribution. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal for HgTe sits outside the supplied names, Zhang is deceased, Hasan's three-dimensional work is a separate achievement, and the 2016 prize touched topological phases. A trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is workable but leaves a contested boundary, whereas B015 has no comparable gap in the supplied credit. I do not rank it above B015, but it is a serious competitor if the credit question can be resolved.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.

Whether the credit of other lattice-clock groups (for example SYRTE, PTB, NIST/JILA collaborators) undermines a two-person configuration; I have not independently verified the detailed priority record.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before awarding the clock work.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle physics) concern cosmic-ray and gamma-ray instrumentation and do not overlap with the optical clock, moire materials or cold-atom candidates on the shortlist.
